analysis.one_liner: Requires government approval of airline slot and route transfers, honors tickets when airlines go bankrupt, and eases foreign ownership limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in January 1993 with a single cosponsor, it was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee and died there when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made airlines get Transportation Department approval before selling international route rights or large blocks of takeoff-and-landing slots at congested airports, letting rival airlines bid. It would have required other airlines to carry stranded passengers' tickets when an airline goes bankrupt, and started a review of frequent flyer practices. It also would have let foreign investors buy up to 49% of a U.S. airline's voting stock, up from the existing 25% limit.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers gain the most: if their airline goes bankrupt, other airlines flying the same routes would have to honor their tickets at no extra charge, instead of leaving them with worthless paper as happened in past airline failures. Travelers at congested airports could benefit from more competition, since incumbent airlines could no longer quietly sell their slots and route rights without rival carriers getting a chance to bid. Frequent flyer members would gain from a review of whether airlines must set aside enough award seats and disclose program changes. Smaller and competing airlines gain from the bidding process and from competition-enhancing factors the Secretary must weigh.

how_it_helps.text: If an airline goes bankrupt, other carriers flying the same routes would have to transport its ticket holders on a space-available basis at no extra charge, protecting passengers from losing the value of tickets they already bought.

Airlines could not transfer international route certificates or ten or more slots at a slot-controlled airport without Transportation Department approval, and rival carriers would get a formal chance to submit competing bids, with the Secretary required to weigh strengthening smaller carriers and preventing concentration in the industry.

The Transportation Department would have to open a rulemaking on whether airlines must make enough seats available for frequent flyer award redemptions, give members notice of program changes, and whether miles should be transferable to reduce the programs' anticompetitive effects.

analysis.who_pays: Large incumbent airlines that hold valuable slots at congested airports and international route certificates would bear the cost: their ability to sell those assets on their own terms would be constrained, and rivals could bid for them. Carriers flying routes served by a bankrupt airline would have to carry its stranded ticket holders for free. The foreign-ownership provision, by contrast, would cost U.S. airlines nothing and would mainly expand their access to foreign capital.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large incumbent airlines and slot holders

drawbacks.text: The transfer-approval process could slow or chill sales of slots and route certificates: even a transfer with no competing bids requires a public-interest determination and the Secretary has up to 90 days (extendable by 60) to decide on certificate transfers, which adds uncertainty for carriers trying to restructure.
Requiring carriers to honor a bankrupt rival's tickets free of charge imposes an unfunded obligation on competing airlines, a cost that could be passed through to passengers in fares.

The frequent flyer provisions only require the Secretary to 'consider' and 'initiate a rulemaking' on seat availability, notice, and mileage transferability, so they would not by themselves guarantee any new passenger rights.

Relaxing the foreign ownership limit from 75% to as low as 51% U.S.-owned would benefit foreign investors and airlines, and critics of such changes have historically worried about foreign influence over U.S. carriers, though the bill includes conditions requiring U.S. citizens to hold the top offices, control, and a reciprocal right to invest in the purchaser's home country.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The passenger protections are real but modest: the bankruptcy ticket guarantee directly helps ordinary travelers, while the frequent flyer section only starts a study process. The slot and certificate bidding rules could genuinely open congested markets to competition, but they add regulatory friction and the benefits depend on how aggressively future Transportation Secretaries applied the public-interest factors. The foreign-ownership relaxation is the odd piece out: it mainly serves foreign investors and airlines seeking capital, and sits awkwardly in a bill titled 'passenger protection.' On balance the bill would likely have been a net benefit to travelers, but a modest one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 103rd Congress, referred to the transportation committee, then quietly sent to its aviation subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings, no markups, and no votes until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Oberstar introduced the bill on January 6, 1993, the opening day of the 103rd Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Public Works and Transportation the same day, and on January 19, 1993 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.
One Republican cosponsored the bill; no other members joined.
No further action was ever recorded on the bill, and it never received a subcommittee, committee, or floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large incumbent airlines are better off: they kept unrestricted control over selling their slots at congested airports and international route certificates, faced no obligation to honor a bankrupt rival's tickets, and frequent flyer practices went unexamined. Foreign investors also benefited from the status quo, since the proposal to raise the foreign voting-ownership limit to 49% died with the bill. Airline passengers gained nothing, and when airlines later failed, stranded ticket holders had to rely on voluntary goodwill policies rather than any legal guarantee.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only member of either party to do so.

against.name: House Committee on Public Works and Transportation

against.name: House Subcommittee on Aviation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 19, 1993 and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship by one Democrat and one Republican, but it drew no floor votes and no recorded opposition, so no partisan split can be measured; it simply died in a Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Major incumbent airlines holding slots and international route certificates
industries.note: The bill would have required government approval and opened competing bids whenever these carriers sold ten or more slots at a congested airport or any foreign route certificate, eroding the value and control of assets only a few big airlines hold. It also would have forced them to carry a bankrupt rival's stranded ticket holders for free.

industries.industry: Foreign investors and foreign air carriers
industries.note: The bill would have let foreign persons buy up to 49% of the voting stock of a U.S. airline, versus the existing 75% U.S.-ownership requirement, subject to conditions such as U.S. control of the board and reciprocal access. This serves foreign capital and airlines seeking entry, with no direct passenger benefit.

The competing-bid process for slots and route certificates, and the requirement that the Secretary weigh strengthening smaller carriers and inhibiting concentration, would have given smaller airlines a path into markets dominated by incumbents.
